body_html:
A first date in Spanish can feel like two tests at once: getting to know someone and getting the language right. The good news is that you don’t need perfect grammar. You need a handful of natural phrases, a few good questions and an idea of the little customs that make the evening flow. As a translator, I notice the same thing again and again: warmth and curiosity carry you much further than vocabulary.

Key takeaways
  • Use tú, not usted, on a date. Formality feels distant.
  • Open questions (¿Qué te gusta hacer…?) keep the conversation alive.
  • Whoever invites often pays, but offering to split is always polite.
  • End with a clear, kind line: Me lo pasé muy bien or La pasé muy bien.
{{toc}}

How to ask someone out in Spanish

In Spanish, a date is una cita, the same word used for a doctor’s appointment, so context matters. To date someone is salir con alguien, literally “to go out with someone”.

SpanishEnglishTone
¿Te gustaría tomar un café conmigo?Would you like to get a coffee with me?Light, low pressure
¿Quieres salir conmigo el sábado?Do you want to go out with me on Saturday?Clear, romantic
¿Te gustaría cenar algún día?Do you feel like dinner some time?Common in Spain
¿Tienes planes el viernes?Do you have plans on Friday?Casual opener

If they say yes, a simple ¡Genial! ¿Te parece bien a las ocho? (“Great! Is eight okay for you?”) sets the plan.

Greetings: the first ten seconds

In much of Latin America and Spain, people greet with a kiss on the cheek (un beso): one in most of Latin America, two in Spain. If you are unsure, follow the other person’s lead. Then:

  • ¡Hola! ¿Qué tal? Hi! How are you?
  • Qué bueno verte. It’s great to see you.
  • Estás muy guapa / guapo. You look great. (In many countries linda/lindo sounds softer and very natural.)
{{image:2}}

First date questions in Spanish

Good questions do most of the work on a first date. Choose open ones that invite a story rather than a yes or no.

Getting to know each other

  • ¿A qué te dedicas? What do you do (for work)?
  • ¿Qué te gusta hacer en tu tiempo libre? What do you like doing in your free time?
  • ¿De dónde eres? Where are you from?
  • ¿Tienes hermanos? Do you have brothers or sisters?

Going a little deeper

  • ¿Cuál es el mejor viaje que has hecho? What’s the best trip you’ve taken?
  • ¿Qué te hace feliz últimamente? What’s been making you happy lately?
  • Si pudieras vivir en cualquier lugar, ¿dónde sería? If you could live anywhere, where would it be?

Showing you’re listening

  • ¿En serio? Really?
  • ¡Qué interesante! Cuéntame más. How interesting! Tell me more.
  • Yo también. Me too. / Yo tampoco. Me neither.
{{book:love-slowly}}

Ordering and paying the check

At a café or restaurant you will need a few practical phrases: ¿Qué me recomiendas? (What do you recommend?), Para mí, un café con leche (For me, a latte) and La cuenta, por favor (The check, please).

Customs vary by country and generation. In many places the person who invited is expected to pay, often with Invito yo (“It’s on me”). Offering to split is still polite: ¿Pagamos a medias? or, in many Latin American countries, ¿Dividimos la cuenta?. If the other person insists, a warm Gracias, la próxima invito yo (“Thanks, next time is on me”) is perfect, and it quietly suggests a second date.

Compliments that sound natural

Keep compliments sincere and specific. They land better than big declarations on a first date.

  • Me encanta tu sonrisa. I love your smile.
  • Eres muy divertida / divertido. You’re really fun.
  • Me caes muy bien. I really like you (as a person). A friendly, safe compliment.
  • Me siento muy cómodo / cómoda contigo. I feel very comfortable with you.

Save te quiero for much later. If you’re curious why, see {{link:te-quiero-vs-te-amo|te quiero vs te amo}}. For flirting that stays respectful, read {{link:how-to-flirt-in-spanish|how to flirt in Spanish}}.

{{image:3}}

How to end the date

SituationSpanishEnglish
It went wellLa pasé muy bien (Latin America) / Lo pasé muy bien (Spain)I had a great time
You want to meet again¿Nos vemos otra vez?Shall we see each other again?
Offering to walk them¿Te acompaño a casa?Shall I walk you home?
Polite, no second dateFue un placer conocerte. Cuídate.It was a pleasure meeting you. Take care.

The next day, a short message works well: Gracias por lo de ayer, me encantó. (“Thanks for yesterday, I loved it.”) You’ll find more ideas in {{link:texting-in-spanish|texting in Spanish}}.

Common mistakes on a first date in Spanish

  • Using usted. It sounds like a job interview. Use tú unless you are in a very formal context.
  • Saying estoy excitado. It usually has a sexual meaning. Say Estoy emocionado / emocionada or Tenía muchas ganas de verte.
  • Translating “I like you” as me gusta tú. The correct form is me gustas, because the person is what pleases you.
  • Rushing te amo. Even te quiero is usually too soon on a first date.

The word cita itself is a good reminder that Spanish words often carry several meanings; the Real Academia Española dictionary lists them all. For more situations like this one, from meeting family to small talk, see {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|my guide to Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

Final thoughts

A first date in Spanish doesn’t need flawless grammar. Ask good questions, listen closely, laugh at your own mistakes and say thank you at the end. People remember how you made them feel, not whether you used the subjunctive.

faq.q: How do you say “date” in Spanish?
faq.a: A romantic date is una cita, and to date someone is salir con alguien. Cita also means an appointment, so context makes the meaning clear.

faq.q: Should I use tú or usted on a date?
faq.a: Use tú. Usted sounds formal and distant in a romantic context, unless you are on a very formal occasion or the other person clearly prefers it.

faq.q: Who pays on a first date in Spanish-speaking countries?
faq.a: It varies by country and generation. Often the person who invited pays, but offering to split with ¿Pagamos a medias? is always polite.
